chapter_theme: High birth as a set of obligations and marks: integrity, shame, truthfulness, generous speech and giving, held to even in poverty. The chapter speaks as if birth produced these qualities, while its own tests make conduct the evidence of birth, and the commentators pull hard in opposite directions on that point.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the nature of the well-born (951-953), they don't change even in poverty (954-956), the disgrace that follows change (957-958), and what lineage requires (959-960).

951.reading: Only in those born to a good house do integrity and shame exist together, naturally.
951.nuance: இயல்பாக and ஒருங்கு both limit the claim: it is about these qualities coming naturally and together, which leaves open whether others can acquire them.

positions.position: Birth decides: others can be taught these qualities but won't keep them for long.
Conduct defines birth: only those with these qualities can be regarded as high-born.
positions.quote: மற்றவர்களை உயர்ந்த குடியில் பிறந்தவர்களாகக் கருத முடியாது.

952.reading: Those of good birth don't slip in these three: conduct, truthfulness and shame.
952.nuance: Parimelazhagar maps the three onto body, speech and mind, and adds that this comes without learning. Manakkudavar takes நாண் physically, as covering one's nakedness, while Kalaignar has honour instead and again makes these the test of who counts as high-born.

953.reading: A smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning: these four, they say, belong to a truly good lineage.
953.nuance: None of the four is about ancestry, and all are ways of treating someone else. Parimelazhagar specifies the setting: when the destitute come, for everyone scorns those who have nothing. That turns etiquette into a test.

954.reading: Even if they gain crores upon crores, the well-born do nothing that diminishes them.
954.nuance: பெறினும் can mean holding wealth or being offered it. Parimelazhagar and Pope lean toward the first, and Kalaignar toward a bribe, which makes this a claim about being unbuyable.

955.reading: Even when what they can give has shrunk, an old family doesn't part from its nature.
955.nuance: The verse measures their poverty by what they can give, not by what they have. Parimelazhagar explains பழங்குடி with the Chera, Chola and Pandya, excellent since creation, which ties this to royal houses.

956.reading: Those who say 'we will live holding to our spotless lineage' will not do unworthy things through deceit.
956.nuance: என்பார் makes lineage a resolve: it applies to those who declare they will live by it. That moves lineage from something one has to something one takes on. Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'.

957.reading: A fault in the well-born stands out high, like the spot on the moon in the sky.
957.nuance: A cost of height: the fault is not larger, but more visible. Each part maps: lineage to sky, virtues to moon, fault to spot. Manakkudavar draws the practical moral.

958.reading: If want of affection shows in one of a good house, people will have doubts about his lineage.
958.nuance: The chapter's claim protects itself here: when a well-born man is cruel, the doubt falls on his birth and not on the rule that birth gives virtue. Reading conduct as evidence of birth also makes the doubt a slur on his parentage, which is not stated.

959.reading: A sprout shows what lies in the ground; the words from the mouth show the lineage of the one born in it.
959.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the disguise: it looks as if the verse is teaching how to identify lineage, but it is really a command to speak sweetly. Note கால், a sprout: the evidence appears at the earliest moment. Kalaignar's version has the mature crop.

960.reading: If you want goodness, want shame; if you want lineage, want humility toward all.
960.nuance: வேண்டின் treats lineage as something one can want and go after. This is the verse most at odds with 951, since a thing given by birth need not be wanted.

positions.position: யார்க்கும் means everyone who is due deference, such as priests, the worthy, ascetics and parents, shown by rising and going to meet them.
யார்க்கும் means all people without limit.

links.note: 951 says that integrity and shame come naturally only to the well-born. 972 says birth is alike for all beings and distinction arises from deeds. This is the Kural's sharpest internal disagreement on lineage, and Kalaignar's reversal of 951 can be read as an attempt to harmonize it with 972.

957 makes the moon's spot the emblem of a visible fault. 1117 asks whether the woman's face, like the moon, carries a spot, and implies it doesn't. The same mark serves moral exposure in one book and the lover's denial of imperfection in another.

In 91 sweet speech comes from a love-soaked and guileless mind. 959 uses speech as a sign of what lies underneath, as the sprout shows the soil. Together they make speech a surface that discloses the source.

223 says that giving before a poor man can utter 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born. 955 takes the giver's own means shrinking, and holds his nature constant. Giving is the chapter's real measure of lineage in both.
133 says conduct itself is lineage and lapse is low birth. 958 is less radical, since lapse leads people to doubt a man's birth, which keeps birth as the underlying fact while 133 dissolves it.

source_issues: 951: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads இப்பிறந்தார் where the verse has இற்பிறந்தார், apparently a transcription error.
955: Parimelazhagar's text repeats விளக்கம் with a stray parenthesis, suggesting a formatting fault.
958: Pope's couplet supplies 'some goodly name', which is not what commentators take நலம் to be.
